The second is the timing mismatch between debits and credits, which is what turnover measures; a business with a 1.69 day turnover has no buffer to absorb a one-day settlement slip, so the schedule's day of the week is a credit decision. The third is the difference between an average and a distribution: ninety days of statements can support an average that no single month achieves, which is why the trough month, not the mean, sets the remittance. A schedule sized to the mean will run clean for three quarters and return in the fourth, and a return is not a small event because the contract converts it into fees, a late charge and, at two returns, a default.
depth.secondExample: The same contractor in a seasonal year shows why the average is the wrong base. Three winter months produce $72,373.34 of net cash each, and nine months produce $31,466.67 each, for $500,320.05 across the year and an annual average of $41,693.34 a month. A remittance sized at 70 percent of the annual average is $29,185.34 a month, or $6,735.08 a week, which is comfortable in January and impossible in July, when net cash is $31,466.67 and the payment would consume 92.75 percent of it before rent. The correct base is the trough: 70 percent of $31,466.67 is $22,026.67 a month, or $5,083.08 a week, which is $64.92 a week less than the proposed $5,148.00 and is the difference between a schedule that survives the slow months and one that produces two returns in a July. The seasonal structure also argues for a share-of-receipts schedule rather than a fixed debit, which Lesson 68 covered; the coverage arithmetic is what tells you whether to make that argument at all.
depth.mistake: Four habits account for most coverage failures. Using gross deposits as revenue, which counts transfers and loan proceeds as trading cash. Sizing the remittance on a monthly average that no month reaches. Ignoring existing debt service, which on a consolidation file is the whole reason the new payment looks affordable. And treating the average daily balance as a reserve, when a 1.69 day turnover means it is a snapshot of money in transit. The diagnostic is a five-line ladder in a fixed order, gross deposits, operating debits, net, existing commitments, residual, computed for the trough month and not the average. If the residual after owner drawings is a small fraction of the remittance, the schedule is fine in good months and a default in bad ones, and the honest recommendation says so before the first debit rather than after the second return.
depth.application: Work the ladder for one file and compute the maximum weekly remittance at a 70 percent coverage test on the trough month. On the worked file: gross deposits $428,200.00, operating debits $396,733.33, net $31,466.67, existing debt service nil after the payoff, available $31,466.67, 70 percent is $22,026.67 a month, divided by 4.333 weeks is $5,083.08 a week, which is $64.92 below the proposed $5,148.00. Then test the calendar: the day of the debit, the processor's settlement cycle, the payroll date, and the number of days of receipts in transit at that hour. Write two sentences for the file: the schedule is 70.89 percent of trough free cash and leaves $9,158.67 a month, and the debit should fall on the day after the largest settlement batch rather than the day before it.
depth.summary: Coverage is a fraction with free cash in the denominator, and free cash is a ladder, not a deposit total. On the worked file $1,190,200.00 of debits against $1,284,600.00 of deposits leaves $31,466.67 a month, a $5,148.00 weekly debit takes 70.89 percent of it, and a 1.69 day turnover means the average balance is not a reserve. Size the payment on the trough month, keep $42,820.00 of weekend settlements in mind when choosing the debit day, and disclose both percentages in the same line.

readings.title: eCFR, 12 CFR Part 1005, Regulation E
readings.note: Read the scope section at 1005.3 and note that the regulation protects consumer accounts rather than business accounts. Read it to see the boundary clearly, because the boundary is what this lesson is about: the merchant's protection on a business account comes from the authorisation and the schedule, not from the error-resolution timetable. A sole proprietor using a personal account may fall inside the rule, which is a question for the merchant's bank.

readings.title: Stripe documentation, reports and settlement timing
readings.note: Read the description of how settlement timing and payout reporting work for a card processor, which is the practical source of the lag this lesson measures. Processor documentation describes one platform's implementation and is not a rule; the merchant's own processor statement is the document that governs its account.

readings.title: Federal Reserve Small Business Credit Survey
readings.note: Read the survey's definitions of credit demand and financing outcomes and the reported experience of firms that applied for funding, which is useful context for why coverage discipline matters to a merchant's next application. Survey data describes populations, not a particular file, and should never be quoted as a prediction about one merchant.

readings.title: IRS Publication 334, Tax Guide for Small Business
readings.note: Read the gross receipts discussion to see why a tax return's receipts and a bank statement's deposits are different quantities, which is the reconciliation Lesson 104 covered and this lesson depends on. US federal tax guidance, current tax year only.

visual.title: Coverage ladder and debit-day gate
visual.description: A five-rung ladder from gross deposits to residual cash, followed by a gate that selects a debit day against the processor's settlement cycle.
steps: Rung 1, gross deposits: $428,200.00 a month, labelled as credits and not revenue, with transfers and proceeds flagged for removal.
Rung 2, operating debits: $396,733.33, giving net operating cash of $31,466.67 and a debit-to-deposit ratio of 92.65 percent.
Rung 3, existing commitments: debt service nil after the payoff, owner drawings $6,000.00, leaving $3,158.67 after a $22,308.00 remittance.
Rung 4, trough test: 70 percent of trough net is $22,026.67 a month or $5,083.08 a week, which is $64.92 below the proposed debit.

Gate, debit day: compare the proposed day with the processor's settlement cycle, the payroll date and the $42,820.00 of weekend settlements in transit, and move the debit to the day after the largest settlement batch.
Output node: a schedule, a day of the week, and two percentages with their denominators stated in one line.

lessons.title: The clauses that fail: acceleration at will, confessed judgment, forced arbitration and the economics of a claim too small to bring
lessons.explanation: Lesson 102 taught how to read the clauses that change the number; this lesson addresses the clauses that change the forum, because a merchant's real position is the arithmetic of enforcing a right rather than the right itself. Four families matter. The first is acceleration, including the 'at will' and 'deems itself insecure' forms; the uniform commercial code does not strike those words, it construes them, so the power exists only where the party in good faith believes the prospect of payment or performance is impaired. The second is confessed judgment, an affidavit in which the debtor consents to entry of judgment without a suit; its effect is to remove the courthouse from the dispute, and several states have restricted or banned the device in recent years, so the governing statute and the date matter. The third is arbitration, which is generally enforceable under the federal statute and which becomes decisive when the forum is distant and the merchant must advance a share of the arbitrator's compensation. The fourth is cost shifting: attorney-fee provisions, indemnities and filing-deposit requirements that convert a $9,400.00 dispute into a $31,950.00 project. That last number is the lesson. A merchant with a $9,400.00 overcharge who must advance $12,500.00 toward an arbitrator, pay $18,000.00 of counsel and spend $1,450.00 travelling is facing a 3.40 to 1 ratio, and a rational merchant abandons the claim. The clause has not defeated the claim in court; it has defeated it in the merchant's own arithmetic, which is the effect the clause was drafted to produce. The advisor's job is to make that arithmetic visible before signature and to record which clauses a lawyer should read, not to pronounce on whether any of them would be enforced.
lessons.example: A trucking company disputes $9,400.00 of charges that it says were taken twice. The contract accelerates the entire balance if the funder deems itself insecure, waives a jury, requires arbitration in a city 1,900 miles away, and provides that each party bears its own costs but that the merchant must advance half of the arbitrator's compensation. The merchant's owner is confident he is right, and he probably is. The arithmetic is what decides the matter. The filing deposit is estimated at $12,500.00. Counsel for a contested commercial arbitration runs $18,000.00, and travel and two nights of hotel for a hearing are $1,450.00. The total is $31,950.00 to pursue $9,400.00. Even a full recovery leaves a loss of $22,550.00, before the time cost and before the risk that the arbitrator awards costs against the merchant. Meanwhile the acceleration clause is live: the disputed amount is 6.1 percent of the balance, and the funder's remedy is the whole balance rather than the difference, which is a fifteen-fold relationship between the trigger and the remedy. There are three honest things to tell the merchant. He can pay the $9,400.00 under protest and preserve the record, which is often the cheapest resolution. He can ask the funder for a written waiver of the arbitration clause for this dispute, which costs an email and sometimes works. He can consult a lawyer about whether the clause is enforceable where the contract is governed, which is a question of law and not one an advisor may answer. What he should not be told is that the clause is void, or that a court will certainly refuse to enforce it, because neither statement is his advisor's to make.
lessons.question: A merchant with a $9,400.00 dispute faces a $12,500.00 arbitration deposit, $18,000.00 of counsel and $1,450.00 of travel. What is the correct way to describe this to him?
lessons.answer: As a 3.40 to 1 cost-to-claim ratio that makes the claim economically irrational to pursue even if it is meritorious, with the three practical options named: pay under protest and preserve the record, request a written waiver of the clause for this dispute, or take advice on enforceability from a lawyer in the governing jurisdiction.
lessons.distractor: As an unenforceable clause, since a term that makes a $9,400.00 claim cost $31,950.00 to bring is unconscionable, and the merchant can therefore sue locally and recover his costs.
lessons.correction: The advisor's error is to convert an economic observation into a legal conclusion. Arbitration clauses are generally enforced under the federal statute, cost-shifting arguments are fact-specific, and unconscionability is a defence argued on the merchant's circumstances rather than a rule about ratios. What the advisor can state with confidence is the arithmetic: $31,950.00 against $9,400.00, a ratio of 3.40, and the fact that acceleration exposes the balance rather than the disputed amount. That is enough to let the merchant decide, which is the point.

depth.definitions: Acceleration is the declaration that the whole unpaid balance is due immediately. An insecurity clause is the contractual trigger for acceleration, and the statutory construction confines it to a good-faith belief that the prospect of payment or performance is impaired. A confessed judgment is an affidavit by the debtor authorising entry of judgment without litigation, filed with a court clerk, and it typically must state the sum, the county, the residence of the parties and the facts out of which the debt arose, depending on the state. An arbitration clause commits disputes to a private decision-maker and is generally enforceable under the federal statute, subject to defences that apply to any contract. A forum-selection clause fixes where a suit must be brought. A cost-shifting provision allocates fees and expenses, and it is the provision that most often decides a small claim, because it changes the price of asserting a right rather than the right itself. This is US material; arbitration and confessed judgment are governed by federal statute and state law respectively, and the state rules differ materially.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism is not one of invalidity but of price. Acceleration converts a small dispute into a large exposure, because the remedy is the balance rather than the arrears: a $10,296.00 shortfall on a $154,440.00 balance is a fifteen-fold relationship, and the merchant's incentive to contest a $500.00 fee is measured against a demand for the whole obligation. Arbitration converts a public, local, precedent-generating process into a private, distant, cost-advancing one, and the advance is what bites: a merchant asked for $12,500.00 before a hearing has to fund the process out of working capital that is already committed. Confessed judgment converts the dispute into a filing, so the merchant's first knowledge of the judgment may be a frozen account, and the remedy is a motion to vacate with an undertaking rather than a defence at trial. Cost shifting then allocates the residue. Each mechanism operates before any court has considered the merits, which is why an advisor who measures only the merits has measured the least important part of the file.
depth.secondExample: One more clause family produces losses without any dispute at all. A twelve-month agreement with an evergreen renewal, a 60-day notice window before the anniversary, a minimum repayment of 40 percent of the advance on renewal, and a $7,500.00 early-termination fee. The merchant plans to refinance in month thirteen, having paid 100 percent of the first term, and discovers that the agreement renewed on month twelve for a second term with a minimum repayment of $31,200.00 on a $78,000.00 advance, and that terminating now costs $7,500.00 plus the minimum. Nothing about this is ambiguous: the notice window was 60 days, the merchant gave none, and the renewal was automatic. The arithmetic is what the merchant needed to see at signature: a 60-day window means the decision date is 305 days into a 365-day term, and the cost of missing it is $38,700.00. The clause did not fail the merchant, the calendar did. This is also the clause most likely to appear in a merchant's own supplier contracts, which is why a merchant with forty vendor agreements can be exposed on any of them, and why the payment-direction register in Lesson 114 belongs beside a renewal calendar in the same file.
depth.mistake: Answering a legal question with an opinion is the mistake that generates the others. A broker who says a clause is unenforceable, or that a jury waiver will never hold, or that confessed judgment is illegal in the merchant's state, is guessing about the law in a specific jurisdiction on a specific date and is doing it in a document that may later be produced. The second mistake is to describe the clause and stop, leaving the merchant with a fact and no arithmetic; the useful version states the deposit, the counsel estimate, the travel, the total and the ratio, and then names the options. The third is to miss the clauses that operate without a dispute, the evergreen renewal and the notice window, because they never appear in a litigation conversation. A file that has been read properly has a clause register with four columns: what the clause does, what it costs to test it, what the merchant must do and by when, and which of those questions requires a lawyer.
depth.application: Compile a clause register for one contract and price the two most consequential clauses. For acceleration, record the trigger, the balance it exposes, and the ratio of exposure to the likely arrears: $154,440.00 against $10,296.00 is 15.0 to 1. For arbitration, record the forum, the distance, the deposit, the estimated counsel cost, the travel and the ratio to the claim: $12,500.00 plus $18,000.00 plus $1,450.00 is $31,950.00, which is 3.40 times $9,400.00. For the evergreen clause, record the notice window, the decision date as a day number in the term, the renewal minimum and the termination fee: a 60-day window in a 365-day term makes day 305 the decision date, and missing it costs $38,700.00. Then write the three questions for the lawyer and keep the advisor's own conclusions out of the file.
depth.summary: Clauses that fail rarely fail in court; they fail in the merchant's arithmetic. Acceleration exposes the whole balance for a small arrears, arbitration moves the dispute to a distant private forum with an advance deposit, confessed judgment removes the courthouse, and cost shifting allocates what is left. Price each one: 15.0 to 1 on acceleration, 3.40 to 1 on the arbitration, $38,700.00 for a missed 60-day notice window. Record what the clause does, what it costs to test, and which question belongs to a lawyer.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 1-309, Option to accelerate at will
readings.note: Read the single sentence and its official comment: a term that allows acceleration at will or when a party deems itself insecure is construed to require a good-faith belief that the prospect of payment or performance is impaired. This is the clearest example in the course of a clause that is read down rather than struck, which is why the advisor describes the construction instead of predicting the outcome.

readings.title: United States Code, Title 9, chapter 1, General provisions (Federal Arbitration Act)
readings.note: Read sections 1 to 4 on the validity and enforcement of arbitration agreements and on stays of litigation. The statute is short and it is the reason an arbitration clause is a forum decision rather than a drafting flourish. Federal statute; state arbitration acts run in parallel and can differ.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 2-302, Unconscionable contract or clause
readings.note: Read the section and note its scope: it applies to transactions in goods, so it is not the rule that governs a financing contract. It is included because it is the provision most often invoked by analogy in these arguments, and the analogy is borrowed reasoning rather than authority, which is the distinction Lesson 110 required a packet to state.

visual.title: Clause register and cost-of-testing gate
visual.description: A four-column register for the clauses that change the forum, with a gate that asks whether testing the clause costs more than the claim and routes the merchant to pay under protest, request a waiver, or seek legal advice.
steps: Column 1, what the clause does: accelerate the balance, remove the courthouse, move the forum 1,900 miles, or shift costs.
Column 2, what it exposes: $154,440.00 of balance on a $10,296.00 arrears, a ratio of 15.0 to 1.
Column 3, what it costs to test: $12,500.00 deposit plus $18,000.00 counsel plus $1,450.00 travel equals $31,950.00, a ratio of 3.40 to 1 against a $9,400.00 claim.
Gate, is the cost of testing greater than the claim: yes sends the merchant to pay under protest, request a written waiver, or take advice; no sends the claim to the dispute process.
Column 4, which question belongs to a lawyer: enforceability in the governing jurisdiction, and nothing else on the page.

lessons.title: Fraud indicators in a merchant file: what to measure, what to write, and what a broker may not say
lessons.explanation: Lesson 71 established the claim ledger and what silence in a file hides; this lesson is about the specific measurements that separate a weak file from a fabricated one, and about the conduct rules that apply once you suspect the second. Indicators fall into five families. Identity: the age of the entity, the age of the operating account, the address, the signer, and whether the person on the application is the person on the identification. Document integrity: creation timestamps, fonts, pagination, running balances that do not carry, and statements whose arithmetic is too clean. Revenue plausibility: growth rates, revenue per employee, average ticket, and the relationship between receipts and the deposits that should represent them. Behaviour: urgency, refusal to permit a bank verification, a willingness to pay a fee before any document is produced, and multiple simultaneous applications. Payment behaviour: existing returns, stacked positions and a balance that moves in round numbers. On the worked file the measurements are a revenue rise from $412,000.00 to $1,401,000.00, which is 240.05 percent, an operating account opened 41 days before the application, three statement PDFs with identical creation timestamps, and a tax return whose receipts exceed the statement deposits by $116,400.00, with deposits at 91.69 percent of reported receipts. None of those is proof of anything. Together they describe a file that should not be submitted, and the discipline is to write the measurement and not the conclusion. A note that says the revenue growth is 240.05 percent and the account is 41 days old is a record. A note that says the merchant is a fraudster is a defamation risk and, if the merchant is in fact a fraudster, a gift to their lawyer.
lessons.example: A staffing company applies for $150,000.00 with a story about a new hospital contract. The file arrives complete, which is itself unusual: statements, returns, a lease, a certificate of insurance and a letter from the hospital. Three measurements fail. First, the statements' three PDFs share a creation timestamp to the second, and the running balance on page two of the July statement does not carry from page one: it is off by $12,040.00. Second, the deposits in the statements are $107,050.00 a month against receipts of $116,750.00 a month on the return, a gap of $9,700.00 a month, or $116,400.00 over the year, and the gap is described as a second account that never appears. Third, the account was opened 41 days before the application, and the hospital letter is undated. The merchant's response to a request for bank verification is that the bank's portal is down and a statement printout will have to do. At that point the advisor stops. The correct actions are four. Record each measurement with its date and its source. Decline to submit and say so in one sentence that states the file does not meet the submission standard, without adjectives. Do not request the missing account and do not suggest which document would resolve the gap, because that is coaching and it converts a detected file into a cleaned one. And do not tell the merchant what a bank may or may not report, because that conversation is prohibited in the other direction. The file goes into a declined register with the indicators and the date, and it stays there.
lessons.question: A file shows 240.05 percent revenue growth, a 41-day-old operating account, three PDFs with identical creation timestamps and a $116,400.00 gap between receipts and deposits. The merchant offers to explain the gap. What do you do?
lessons.answer: Stop the submission, record the four measurements with their dates and sources, decline in writing in factual terms, and decline to discuss what documentation would resolve the gap, because soliciting the reconciling document is coaching and coaching is what turns a detected file into a clean one.
lessons.distractor: Take the explanation, request the missing account statements so the deposits reconcile to the return, and submit once the numbers agree, since a reconciled file is what underwriting needs and the advisor is not the underwriter.
lessons.correction: The request for the reconciling statements is the misconduct, not the submission. It tells the merchant which measurement failed, and the next version of the file will satisfy it. The other error is the framing that the advisor is a conduit and therefore not responsible: a person who prepares or presents a document they believe to be false is exposed independently of the funder's decision, and the record of what was known and when is the only protection available afterwards. The correct note is a measurement, a date and a decision, not an accusation and not a suggestion.

depth.definitions: An indicator is an observation that raises the probability of a misstatement without proving one. Document integrity means the internal consistency of a document: metadata, pagination, fonts, arithmetic and running balances. A synthetic identity is a persona assembled from real and fabricated elements, often a legitimate employer identification number combined with a fabricated owner and a virtual address. A straw signer is a person who signs for a business they do not control. Coaching is any suggestion by an advisor about which document or which figure would improve a file's chance of approval. Tipping off is the disclosure that a suspicious activity report has been filed or is under consideration, and the prohibition binds financial institutions and the people who work for them; an advisor who learns of a report should treat it as information that cannot be relayed. Scope: US federal rules, with state licensing and consumer protection statutes running alongside.
depth.mechanism: The mechanism that matters here is that fabrication is usually visible in consistency rather than in any single figure. A real business has variance: deposits do not reconcile to receipts to the dollar, growth is uneven across months, and statement metadata reflects the dates the statements were actually produced. A fabricated file is often too consistent, because the fabricator controls every number and has no reason to introduce the noise that reality provides. That is why three identical creation timestamps and a zero-variance reconciliation are stronger indicators than a large revenue jump on their own. The second mechanism is the economics of detection: a funder that declines a file loses a fee, so the incentive to look past an indicator is real, and the advisor's independence is the only check in the process that is not paid on approval. The third is documentary: every action taken after suspicion becomes evidence, so the note written on the day, with the measurement and the source, is worth more than any explanation written afterwards.
depth.secondExample: A different file shows the pattern that detection systems are built for. A business applies for $150,000.00 with an entity formed eleven weeks earlier, a virtual office address that the same suite shares with thirty-nine other registrations, an owner whose identification photograph is a different person from the signer on the lease, and four applications to four different funders within six days, totalling $600,000.00. No single element is decisive: new businesses borrow, virtual offices are legitimate, and shopping is rational. The pattern is the product of the four, and the request for $600,000.00 across six days against eleven weeks of history is the measurement that makes it legible. The advisor's correct entry is a dated note listing the formation date, the address, the identification discrepancy and the four applications with their dates, and a decision not to submit. The incorrect entry is any sentence that characterises the applicant's intent. If the file later turns out to be genuine, the note is still accurate, which is the test of a well-written indicator record.
depth.mistake: Indicator handling fails in three ways, and each has a commercial cause. Submitting a file with indicators because the funder will decide, which shifts a decision the advisor is competent to make onto a party that cannot see the advisor's conversation. Coaching, which is any version of 'if you can show me the other account, this will work', and which converts an indicator into a training exercise. And characterising, which writes 'fraud', 'liar' or 'fake' into a document that may be produced in litigation, when the same information written as a measurement is both more useful and safer. Underneath all three is a commercial pressure the advisor should name: a file with a $150,000.00 advance generates a fee, and the fee is the reason a doubtful file gets submitted. The discipline is to keep a declined register with the measurements and the dates, so that the decision is a record rather than a conversation, and so that a pattern across files becomes visible before a regulator finds it.
depth.application: Choose one file and build an indicator sheet with five columns: family, measurement, source and date, what would explain it innocently, and what document would settle it. On the worked file the rows are revenue growth 240.05 percent against a prior year of $412,000.00; account age 41 days; three PDFs with one creation timestamp; a $116,400.00 receipts-to-deposits gap, or $9,700.00 a month; and an undated third-party letter. The innocent explanations belong in the sheet because they are what a fair reviewer would want to see, and the settling documents are for the file and not for the merchant. Then write the decline note in three sentences: what was observed, when, and that the file does not meet the submission standard. Keep the sheet in the declined register. If the same address or the same signer appears again, the register is what tells you.
depth.summary: Fraud indicators are measurements, not conclusions. Identity age, document integrity, revenue plausibility, behaviour and payment history each contribute, and fabrication usually shows as too much consistency rather than as one impossible number. Record what was seen, with dates and sources; decline in factual language; never coach the merchant toward a document that would fix the measurement; and never relay anything about a report a financial institution may file. The declined register is the asset that comes out of a file you refused.

readings.title: FinCEN, suspicious activity report advisory on key terms
readings.note: Read the definitions of key terms and the description of what a report is for, which is the context behind the confidentiality rule. FinCEN guidance for financial institutions; a broker is not the filing institution, and this reading explains why the advisor should treat the subject as unmentionable rather than as a fact to share.

readings.title: FinCEN, analysis of identity-related suspicious activity
readings.note: Read the summary of the identity-related typologies FinCEN identified, which maps closely to the indicator families in this lesson: account opening, identification documents, virtual addresses and multiple applications. A news release summarising an analysis, not a rule, and it describes patterns across institutions rather than the facts of any one file.

readings.title: eCFR, 31 CFR 1020.320, Reports by banks of suspicious transactions
readings.note: Read paragraph (e), the confidentiality provision, and note who it binds: the financial institution and its directors, officers, employees and agents. That is the source of the tipping-off rule an advisor must respect when a bank shares information, and it is the reason the correct answer to 'will this be reported' is that the advisor does not discuss it.

readings.title: IRS, identity theft information for businesses
readings.note: Read the description of business identity theft and the signs the IRS lists, which is useful because a merchant whose identity has been used is a victim in the same file where the funder suspects a perpetrator. US federal tax administration guidance.

visual.title: Five-family indicator matrix with a submission gate
visual.description: A matrix that scores five families of indicator on one file, then passes through a gate that asks whether the explanation can be documented without coaching.
steps: Family 1, identity: entity age, account age 41 days, address, signer, and whether the identification matches the person.
Family 2, document integrity: three PDFs with one creation timestamp, a running balance that is off by $12,040.00, and an undated third-party letter.
Family 3, revenue plausibility: growth of 240.05 percent from a $412,000.00 base, and revenue per employee against the staffing model.
Family 4, behaviour: refusal of bank verification, urgency, a fee demanded before documents, and four applications in six days.
Family 5, payment behaviour: existing returns, stacked positions, and round-number balances.

Gate, can the explanation be documented without suggesting a document: no sends the file to the declined register with measurements and dates; yes sends it to underwriting with the explanation attached and sourced.

lessons.title: Complaint routing and the response record: who receives a complaint, what the clock is, and what the log tells you
lessons.explanation: Lesson 89 covered records, retention and answering a disputed debit; this lesson is about the routing decision and the response record, because the same complaint has different consequences depending on where it lands. Four routes matter for a merchant finance file. The state regulator that licenses the funder or the broker, which is the route with the most direct power over the counterparty's ability to trade. The state attorney general, whose consumer and business protection statutes often reach commercial conduct. The Federal Trade Commission, whose general prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce is not limited to consumers, and which takes complaints through a public reporting channel. And the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, whose complaint system is built around consumer products, so a small business credit complaint may fall outside it unless the product is consumer credit or the respondent is a covered institution; the small business lending data rule adds a separate reporting obligation that has its own scope and dates, and a cite to it should always state which version is being relied on. The response discipline is the same on every route. Acknowledge in writing quickly, typically within three business days on your own standard rather than the regulator's. Preserve the documents before anyone edits anything. Answer the facts that can be evidenced and decline to characterise. State what will happen next and by when. And record the complaint in a log that carries a root cause, because a complaint rate without causes is a number that tells you nothing.
lessons.example: A twelve-month log shows three complaints across 214 funded files, which is 1.40 per 100. One alleges a $3,300.00 debit taken eleven days after payoff. One alleges a fee that was not disclosed. One alleges a call after the merchant opted out. Each has a different route and a different remedy. The debit after payoff belongs with the state regulator if the funder is licensed there, because it is a servicing and authorisation failure, and the remedy is a refund and a cancellation step. The fee complaint belongs with the FTC or the attorney general, because it is a disclosure question, and the remedy is a corrected disclosure and a refund if the fee was not authorised. The call complaint is the one that needs counsel, because the telephone rules are written around consumers and their application to a business mobile number is contested. The arithmetic that decides how much attention each deserves is not the count but the population. The payoff control has been running for fourteen months and 46 payoffs have occurred in that window, so a defect in the cancellation step puts 46 files at risk rather than one. The opt-out failure puts every call made after an opt-out at risk, and at one call a month across 214 files that is 12 calls a year, against statutory per-call amounts that a consumer-facing statute sets in the hundreds of dollars. Three complaints, three causes, three populations, and the rate of 1.40 per 100 describes none of them.
lessons.question: A merchant complains about a $3,300.00 debit taken after payoff. The log shows 3 complaints in 214 files and the fee revenue on those 3 files was $12,600.00. How should the complaint be handled and what does the log actually tell you?
lessons.answer: Acknowledge within three business days, preserve the authorisation, payoff quote, wire confirmation and termination demand, refund the debit if the payoff date supports it, and treat the issue as a control failure affecting the 46 payoffs processed in the fourteen months the process has run, not as one of three complaints at a rate of 1.40 per 100.
lessons.distractor: The complaint rate is 1.40 per 100 files and the fee revenue at risk is $12,600.00 against a refund of $3,300.00, so the correct response is to explain the payoff timing, refund nothing, and log the complaint as resolved with the explanation given.
lessons.correction: The rate and the fee revenue are both the wrong unit of analysis. The relevant population is the files that passed through the defective step, which is 46 payoffs, and a refund decision made on one complaint leaves 45 files that may contain the same error. The commercial argument is also backwards: the fee on the three files is $12,600.00, and a regulator's finding on an unauthorised debit can cost a licence condition, which is not measured in refunds. The error a broker makes is to price a complaint against its own fee and to ignore the process that produced it.

depth.definitions: A complaint is an expression of dissatisfaction about a product or a service, and a dispute is a complaint that asserts a specific error and demands a remedy; the two are handled differently because a dispute requires a factual determination. Root cause is the process failure that produced the complaint, as distinct from the individual error. A corrective action is the change to the process, with an owner and a date. A regulator is the agency with authority over the respondent, and authority is the key word: the FTC's reach, a state attorney general's reach and a licensing regulator's reach are different, and the same complaint can be routed to one and not another. The small business lending data rule requires covered financial institutions to collect, report and provide certain data about small business credit applications; its scope and compliance dates have been revised more than once, so any statement about it must name the version and the date. Scope: US federal and state; licensing is state by state and the respondent's licence status is a fact to check rather than assume.
depth.mechanism: Four mechanisms make complaint handling a control function rather than a customer service function. The first is that the route determines the remedy: a licensing regulator can condition or revoke, an attorney general can seek restitution across a class, the FTC can seek injunctive relief and redress, and a court can award damages, so the same facts produce different exposures. The second is that the response clock runs against a record that the complainant already holds, so an inaccurate first response is worse than a slow one. The third is that complaints aggregate: three complaints with one cause are a pattern, and a regulator that receives four complaints about the same fee from four merchants will look for the fifth. The fourth is that the log is the only instrument that converts complaints into process change, and a log without root causes and populations cannot tell you whether the problem is one file or forty-six.
depth.secondExample: The disclosure complaint shows the mechanism at work in a quieter way. A merchant says a $1,950.00 administrative fee was not in the disclosure he was given, and produces a disclosure with eight numbered items and no fee line. The institution's current template has nine items and includes the fee, so the question is which version was in force on the date of his offer. The file contains two versions with no version control and no date, which means neither the merchant nor the funder can prove which was delivered. The remedy is a refund of $1,950.00 and, more importantly, a version control change: every disclosure carries a version number, every file records the version sent and the date, and the delivery method produces a record. The arithmetic that justifies the change is not the single refund. If the template changed in March and 61 offers were issued between March and the date the fee line was added in July, then 61 files are in the same position, and at $1,950.00 a file the exposure is $118,950.00. That is the number the log should produce, and it is only producible if the log records the cause and the population rather than the complaint.
depth.mistake: Complaint handling fails in four places, and all four are procedural rather than attitudinal. Pricing a complaint against the fee earned on the file, which makes every complaint look cheaper to explain than to fix. Answering with a characterisation, such as asserting that the merchant agreed or that the debit was authorised, before checking the documents that would prove it. Treating a single complaint as a single event, when the process that produced it has a population. And routing by habit, sending everything to the funder's customer service address when the licensing regulator is the recipient with leverage. The correction for all four is procedural: a log with date, route, allegation, documents relied on, root cause, population affected, corrective action, owner and closure date, reviewed monthly. A complaint function that cannot produce that table is a complaints inbox, not a control.
depth.application: Keep a complaint log for one firm and compute the exposure it implies. Fields: complaint date, route, allegation in one sentence, files or calls in the affected population, documents preserved, root cause, corrective action, owner, closure date. On the worked log: 3 complaints, 1.40 per 100 files, three causes, populations of 46 payoffs, 61 disclosures and 12 calls, a refund exposure of $3,300.00 plus $1,950.00, and a disclosure exposure of $118,950.00 if the version gap is confirmed. Then write the two sentences for the monthly review: the rate is 1.40 per 100 files and is stable, and the exposure is concentrated in two process failures with populations of 46 and 61, which is where the corrective actions belong. If the log cannot state a population, the root cause has not been found.
depth.summary: A complaint is a routing decision, a clock and a population. The licensing regulator has the most direct power, the attorney general and the FTC reach commercial conduct, and the consumer bureau's system fits consumer products rather than most small business credit. Answer with documents and dates rather than characterisations, count the files that passed through the defective step rather than the complaints received, and keep a log that names a root cause, a population, a corrective action and an owner.

readings.note: Read the list of products the complaint system covers and note how it is framed around consumer financial products, which is why a small business credit complaint often has no home here. The page also describes the response process and typical timing, which is a useful benchmark even where the bureau has no jurisdiction.

readings.title: California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation
readings.note: Read the complaint and licensing pages as an example of a state regulator with both licensing power and a public complaint channel. California is one example among many; the respondent's own state licence and its status are the facts that matter, and they are checkable before a complaint is routed.

visual.title: Complaint routing tree with population sizing
visual.description: A routing tree that sends each allegation to the regulator with the relevant power, then attaches a population count and an exposure to each branch.
steps: Allegation node: a $3,300.00 debit eleven days after payoff, with the payoff quote and wire confirmation requested on day one.
Route A, licensing regulator: the funder's licence in the state, with the power to condition or revoke, and the remedy a refund plus a cancellation control.
Route B, attorney general or FTC: disclosure and conduct allegations, with restitution and injunctive remedies, not limited to consumers.
