Log node: root cause, corrective action, owner, closure date, monthly review.

lessons.title: Capstone: the ninety-day post-closing audit, ten checks and thirty cells
lessons.explanation: The level's first four lessons produced documents and its fifth produced an arithmetic test; this capstone uses them to answer a single question at day ninety: is the file performing as the documents say it would, and where does it diverge? Ten checks, each with a document, a test and a status, and each status recorded as pass, exception or unresolved. One, the settlement reconciliation: approved amount, itemised deductions and wire, tied to the bank credit, with the escrow release date recorded. Two, the first debit: its date measured against the contract's definition of the funding date, not against the date the merchant signed. Three, the amortisation: count and amount of debits against the schedule, with the remaining balance recomputed rather than read from the servicer's screen. Four, the return register: every code, every permitted action, every fee, and whether the fees were actually credited to the balance. Five, the authorisation: whether the party debiting the account is the party the merchant authorised, which is the check that catches an assignment nobody papered. Six, the filing: effective, continued where a continuation window is open, and terminated where the obligation is discharged. Seven, the disclosure: which version was delivered, on what date, by what method. Eight, the calendar: whether the debit day still sits after the settlement batch and outside the seasonal trough. Nine, the exit: whether a payoff quote, a per diem and a termination path are ready before the merchant asks for them. Ten, the record: complaints, calls and the outreach log, with a decision line at the end. Ten checks with three fields each is thirty cells, and a professional audit answers all thirty rather than the ones that flatter the file.
lessons.example: The file funded on Friday 7 November at $156,000.00, a 1.32 factor and $205,920.00 in forty weekly debits of $5,148.00 is audited on Friday 6 February, after thirteen scheduled debits. Check one passes: $156,000.00 approved, less $46,507.05 of itemised deductions and a $7,800.00 escrow, is a wire of $101,692.95, which ties to the bank credit, and the escrow was released on day thirty-one with a dated confirmation. Check two passes with a note: the first debit fell on 14 November, seven days after the wire value date of 7 November; had the contract defined funding as the date of acceptance rather than the value date, the debit would have been four days early. Check three: thirteen debits of $5,148.00 is $66,924.00, and the recomputed balance is $205,920.00 less $66,924.00, which is $138,996.00, matching the servicer to the dollar. Check four fails by $100.00: the bank shows fifteen debit entries totalling $77,220.00 and two credits of $5,148.00, so the net movement is $66,924.00, but two $50.00 return fees were collected separately and never credited, so the true balance is $138,896.00. The variance is 0.07 percent of the balance and 100 percent of the fee line, which is the point: a variance measured against the balance looks immaterial and a variance measured against the account it belongs to is total. Check five passes. Check six passes with a continuation noted. Check seven passes with the version recorded. Check eight is an exception: the debit still falls on Friday and the merchant's processor settles on a two-day cycle, so the entry is collected two days before the week's largest settlement batch, which is the mechanism Lesson 116 measured. Check nine is unresolved until a payoff is requested. Check ten passes: no complaints and one merchant call about the debit day, which is a record that supports the check-eight finding rather than contradicting it.
lessons.question: At day ninety the ledger reconciles to the dollar on debits but two $50.00 return fees were never credited. Is the file clean, and what does the audit do with a $100.00 variance?
lessons.answer: The file is not clean: the true balance is $138,896.00 rather than $138,996.00, and the $100.00 is an exception because it is 100 percent of the fee line even though it is 0.07 percent of the balance; the audit records it as an exception with the fee line as its population, corrects the balance, and tests whether the same failure occurred on other files.
lessons.distractor: The file is clean because the debits reconcile to the dollar and $100.00 is below any reasonable materiality threshold, so the audit records a passing status with a note for the next scheduled review.
lessons.correction: Materiality measured against the balance is the wrong comparison, because the fee line is its own account and a fee that was collected and not credited will produce a payoff shortfall at the end of the term, which is exactly the residual that suspends a termination duty. The audit's job is to find the failure while it is $100.00 rather than at payoff, when it is a stalled transaction. The second half of the answer matters as much: an exception on one file is a question about the population, and the population is every returned debit in the portfolio.

depth.definitions: A post-closing audit is a dated review of a funded file against the documents that created it. A check is a single question with a named document, a test and a status. A status is pass, exception or unresolved, and unresolved is a legitimate status rather than a failure to decide. A cell is one field of one check, so ten checks with three fields is thirty cells. The reconciliation identity is approved less itemised deductions less withholdings equals the wire, and separately, total repayment less debits collected equals the balance. Materiality is the threshold at which a variance is treated as significant, and this lesson's rule is that materiality is measured against the account the variance belongs to rather than against the balance. Borrowed reasoning: the SBA's list of events that release it from liability on a guarantee is a published statement that servicing failures move loss from the guarantor to the servicer, and it is cited here for the logic, not as authority over a private file. Scope: US; the SBA material governs guaranteed loans only.
depth.mechanism: The audit works because each check has an independent source. The settlement check compares the contract to the bank, the amortisation check compares the contract to the ledger, the return check compares the ledger to the bank, and the filing check compares the file to a public record. Where two independent sources agree, the cell is a pass; where they diverge, the divergence is the finding. The second mechanism is that the checks are ordered by dependency: a return that was never credited changes the balance, which changes the payoff, which changes whether a termination is owed, so a failure in check four propagates into checks three and nine unless it is caught. The third is population thinking: every exception is a sample of a process, and the audit's value is in converting a $100.00 finding into a question about every return in the portfolio. The fourth is the decision line: an audit that ends with findings and no decision has produced work, not an answer.
depth.secondExample: A second file shows the audit producing a decline rather than a cure. A merchant funded in September at $88,000.00 is audited at day ninety with eleven of thirty-six debits collected, two returns in October, and a disclosure on file with seven numbered items when the governing state's list has nine. The amortisation reconciles, the returns were permitted and the fees were credited, and the settlement ties, so five checks pass. Check seven fails on the disclosure, and the failure is not curable retrospectively: the merchant was never told two items, one of which is the broker's compensation. Check five fails as well, because the funder assigned the file in November and the merchant's authorisation still names the original originator, so a block of entries was debited by a party the merchant never authorised. Two failures and one unresolved item are enough to decline the merchant's request for a second advance, and the audit says why in one line: the file is performing, the documents are not. That distinction is the whole value of the exercise, because a funder that reads only the payment history would renew this merchant and inherit both defects.
depth.mistake: A ninety-day audit fails in five ways, and the most seductive is the first: auditing the ledger against itself, which always reconciles because it is the same data. Measuring materiality against the balance, which makes a fee-line failure invisible. Treating an unresolved cell as a pass, which converts an open question into an implied answer. Missing the authorisation check after an assignment, which is the defect that produces unauthorised returns months later. And ending without a decision line, so the audit becomes a report rather than a determination. The diagnostic is the thirty-cell count: if a reviewer cannot say which of the thirty cells are unanswered, the audit is a narrative. A file that answers twenty-nine of thirty and names the one it cannot answer is in better shape than one that claims thirty and cannot produce the documents.
depth.application: Run the ten checks on one live file and score the thirty cells. Model result on the worked file: settlement pass with the escrow release dated; first debit pass with a note on the funding-date definition; amortisation pass at $138,996.00; returns exception at $100.00, corrected balance $138,896.00, population every return in the portfolio; authorisation pass; filing pass with a continuation date; disclosure pass with a version and a delivery record; calendar exception, because the Friday debit precedes the settlement batch; exit unresolved until a payoff is requested; record pass with one merchant call logged. That is twenty-six passes, two exceptions, one unresolved and one cell still open on the exit check. The decision line reads: the file is performing and two process defects are open, one in fee crediting and one in debit-day selection, neither of which changes the recommendation to continue but both of which must be cured before any renewal is priced.
depth.summary: A ninety-day audit is ten checks, three fields each, and a decision line. The checks work because each compares two independent sources: contract to bank, contract to ledger, ledger to bank, file to public record. Materiality is measured against the account a variance belongs to, so a $100.00 fee failure is total on the fee line even at 0.07 percent of the balance. Name the unanswered cells, convert every exception into a population, and end with a determination rather than a narrative.

readings.title: eCFR, 13 CFR 120.524, When is SBA released from liability on its guarantee
readings.note: Read the ten events, from a material failure to comply with a loan programme requirement to a failure to service or liquidate in a prudent manner to a failure to use the required forms. It is the clearest published statement that servicing failures move loss from the guarantor to the party that serviced the file, and it is the reasoning this capstone borrows. It governs SBA guaranteed loans and does not bind a private funder; cite it as borrowed reasoning with its scope stated.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 9-210, Request for accounting
readings.note: Read subsection (b) and the fourteen-day duty, which is the merchant's instrument for testing a balance the servicer reports. The audit's check three recomputes the balance independently; this section is what makes the servicer's own statement a document the merchant can demand rather than a courtesy.

readings.title: Uniform Commercial Code, section 9-625, Remedies for secured party's failure to comply
readings.note: Read subsection (b) on damages measured by loss, including the cost of or inability to obtain alternative financing, and subsection (f) on the $500 amount for an unanswered accounting request. This is the consequence side of the audit's unresolved cells.

readings.title: eCFR, 13 CFR 120.150, SBA's lending criteria
readings.note: Read the five sentences of the criteria, including the requirement that loans be so sound as to reasonably assure repayment, which is the standard a ninety-day audit is ultimately serving. SBA programme text as amended at 88 FR 21085, not a rule for private lenders.

visual.title: Ten-check audit board with thirty cells and a decision line
visual.description: A board of ten rows and three columns, settlement, first debit, amortisation, returns, authorisation, filing, disclosure, calendar, exit and record, scored pass, exception or unresolved, closing in a decision line.
steps: Rows 1 to 3, money: settlement ties to the bank credit; first debit measured against the contract's funding-date definition; balance recomputed to $138,996.00 and corrected to $138,896.00.
Rows 4 to 6, documents: return register with codes and credited fees; authorisation naming the party actually debiting; filing status with its continuation date.

Rows 7 to 9, conduct: disclosure version and delivery date; debit day against the settlement cycle and the seasonal trough; payoff quote, per diem and termination path ready before they are requested.
Row 10, record: complaints, calls and outreach, with the merchant call about the debit day recorded as support for the row 8 finding.
Score node: twenty-six passes, two exceptions, one unresolved, one open cell, with each exception converted into a population.
Decision line: the file is performing, two process defects are open, and no renewal is priced until both are cured.

questions.prompt: Ninety days of statements show $1,284,600.00 of deposits, $1,190,200.00 of debits and an average daily balance of $22,410.00. A first-position remittance of $5,148.00 a week is proposed, equal to 70.89 percent of monthly net cash. The merchant is profitable and has never bounced a supplier cheque. Why does the first debit still risk an R01, and what measurement shows it?
questions.answer: The account turns over every 1.69 days, so the average balance covers 1.69 days of debits; a Friday debit collected against Monday card settlements that settle at T+2 arrives before roughly $42,820.00 of weekend settlements land, which is a timing failure rather than an insolvency, and the fix is to measure the debit day against the settlement calendar rather than the monthly average.
questions.distractor: The merchant is profitable and the remittance is only 5.21 percent of deposits, so there is no coverage question and an R01 would indicate a bank error rather than a schedule problem.
questions.correction: The two ratios answer different questions. The remittance is 5.21 percent of deposits, which is why the offer looks obviously affordable, and 70.89 percent of net free cash, which is why it consumes almost all of the surplus. Neither ratio captures the third fact: a 92.65 percent debit-to-deposit ratio with a 1.69 day turnover means the balance at any hour is a timing artefact, so the debit date, the settlement lag and the payroll date matter more than the monthly average.

questions.prompt: A merchant wants to contest a $9,400.00 overcharge. The contract accelerates the balance when the funder deems itself insecure and requires arbitration before an arbitrator 1,900 miles away, with the merchant advancing half the arbitrator's compensation, estimated at $12,500.00, plus $18,000.00 of counsel and $1,450.00 of travel. What is the clause doing, and how should it be described?
questions.answer: The acceleration clause is read down to a good-faith belief that the prospect of payment is impaired, so it is not the unlimited trigger it appears to be, while the forum and cost provisions make the dispute cost $31,950.00 to pursue against a $9,400.00 claim, a ratio of 3.40 to 1, so the clause's real function is to make the claim economically irrational; describe that effect and record it, and leave enforceability to a lawyer in the governing jurisdiction.
questions.distractor: The acceleration clause is void because it says at will, and the arbitration clause is unenforceable because it is unconscionable, so the merchant can ignore both and sue locally.
questions.correction: Both conclusions are too strong and both are the kind of conclusion an advisor should not be issuing. Acceleration at will is construed to require good faith rather than struck, and arbitration clauses are generally enforced under the federal statute, with unconscionability a defence a court may or may not accept on these facts. The advisor's product is the arithmetic of the clause: $31,950.00 of cost against a $9,400.00 claim, plus the time, plus the fact that the balance accelerates while the dispute is pending.

questions.prompt: A file shows revenue rising from $412,000.00 to $1,401,000.00 in one year, a bank account opened 41 days before the application, three statement PDFs with identical creation timestamps and a tax return whose receipts are exactly $116,400.00 above the deposits in the statements. The merchant says the statements are 'just missing a couple of accounts'. What do you do, and what do you not say?
questions.answer: Stop the submission, record the specific indicators with their measurements, decline to coach the merchant on what documentation would look better, and leave the account opening and the reporting to the institution; you do not tell the merchant that a suspicious activity report has been or may be filed, and you do not describe the file as fraud in a document that could be produced.
questions.distractor: Ask the merchant to supply the missing account statements so the deposit figure matches the return, then submit once the numbers reconcile, since an unexplained gap of $116,400.00 is a documentation problem rather than an integrity problem.
questions.correction: Asking for the statements that would close the gap is coaching, and coaching converts an indicator into a cleaned file. The indicators are not the size of the gap but the pattern: a 240.05 percent revenue rise, a 41 day old account, identical document creation timestamps and a 91.69 percent deposit-to-receipt ratio that is just close enough to look reconciled. The advisor records what was seen and when, declines to submit, and keeps the note factual, because the tipping-off prohibition and the defamation exposure both run against speculation.

questions.prompt: A merchant complains that a $3,300.00 debit was taken eleven days after the file was paid off. Your twelve-month log shows three complaints across 214 funded files, one about that debit, one about a disclosed fee and one about a call after an opt-out. What is the response and what does the log tell you?
questions.answer: Acknowledge in writing within three business days, preserve the debit authorisation, the payoff quote and the termination demand, refund the debit if the payoff date supports it, and treat the three complaints as 1.40 per 100 files with three distinct root causes, one of which is a control failure at payoff rather than a communication failure.
questions.distractor: The complaint rate is 1.40 per 100 files, which is below any reasonable threshold, so the correct response is to explain the payoff timing to the merchant and log the complaint as resolved without changing the process.
questions.correction: A rate is not a control. The three complaints have three different causes, and the debit after payoff is the one that a process change would have prevented: the payoff and the debit authorisation lived in different systems and nothing cancelled one when the other closed. The response also has to be evidence first, because the merchant's version and the servicer's version will diverge, and the documents that settle it are the dated quote, the wire confirmation and the authenticated demand for termination.

questions.prompt: At day ninety on a $205,920.00 file funded on 7 November, thirteen weekly debits of $5,148.00 were expected. The bank shows fifteen debit entries totalling $77,220.00 and two credits of $5,148.00, plus $140.00 of bank fees and two $50.00 funder return fees that were debited separately. The servicer's ledger shows the balance reduced by $66,924.00. Reconcile it.
questions.answer: The bank movement is $66,924.00 net of the two returns, so the debits reconcile, but the two $50.00 fees were collected and never credited, so the ledger overstates the balance by $100.00; the $140.00 of bank fees belongs to the merchant's own bank and never touches the obligation, and the audit records both facts separately.
questions.distractor: The ledger is correct because $77,220.00 of debits less $10,296.00 of returns is $66,924.00 and the fees of $240.00 are immaterial, so the file closes with no exceptions.
questions.correction: The reconciliation has to separate three ledgers: the bank's, the servicer's and the contract's. The two $50.00 fees were contractually added to the balance and collected, so a ledger that ignores them leaves the merchant owing $100.00 more than the file says and, more importantly, leaves the fee line unaudited for the rest of the term. The $140.00 is the merchant's own bank charge and is not part of the obligation at all, which is exactly the kind of line that gets folded into a payoff and produces the residual that defeats a termination.

questions.prompt: A settlement sheet shows $150,000.00 approved, $46,207.05 of cash deductions and a $7,500.00 escrow. Write the two numbers the merchant needs and the one number that must never be quoted alone.
questions.answer: $96,292.95 reaches the account, $103,792.95 is available once the escrow is released, and the approved $150,000.00 must never be quoted alone because every deducted dollar is borrowed at the 1.34 factor, making the price $52.96 per $100 of net wire against $34.00 per $100 of the approved amount.
questions.distractor: $150,000.00 is the funding amount and the deductions are transaction costs, so the merchant's cost is the $51,000.00 of the factor and the escrow is a fee that reduces the effective proceeds.
questions.correction: Quoting the approved amount alone is the single most common misdescription in this market, because it makes a 1.34 obligation look like a 34 percent price on money the merchant never received. The escrow is not a fee: it is the merchant's own cash held against a condition, so it belongs on the available line and not on the cost line.

questions.prompt: A debit is returned R02, account closed, on a file with 30 of 40 weekly debits outstanding. The servicer's clerk re-presents it the following week. What is wrong, and what is the consequence under a two-returns-in-ninety-days default clause?
questions.answer: An R02 cannot be re-initiated at all, so the re-presentment is itself a rules breach and the second return is the second return in ninety days, which triggers the default clause; the remaining balance of $154,440.00 plus a $1,500.00 default fee becomes demandable, and the guarantor is exposed on $155,940.00.
questions.distractor: The re-presentment is permitted because a closed account can reopen, and the default clause needs two returns on the same debit rather than two returns in the period.
questions.correction: The rules distinguish returns that may be retried from returns that may not: insufficient funds and a few administrative returns permit at most two re-presentments, while account closed, no account, unauthorised and revoked authorisation do not permit re-initiation. Reading the clause as requiring two returns on the same entry converts a clear default trigger into one that never fires, which is how a file drifts into collections without anyone deciding to send it there.

questions.prompt: A payoff is wired two days late, leaving $165.78 outstanding, and the merchant's lawyer demands a termination statement. What are the secured party's duties and what is the merchant's remedy if it does nothing?
questions.answer: The duty to send or file a termination statement runs within twenty days after an authenticated demand and only where no obligation is secured and no commitment to advance remains, so the $165.78 suspends the duty; the merchant's route is to clear the residual, demand again in writing, and, if the secured party still fails, claim the statutory damages plus actual loss.
questions.distractor: The duty runs from the date of payoff regardless of a residual balance, so the secured party is in breach after twenty days and the merchant can treat the financing statement as terminated without further steps.
questions.correction: The condition matters as much as the clock. Termination is owed when there is no secured obligation, and the merchant's own late wire created the obligation that suspends the duty, which is why the residual has to be cleared before the demand is made. A filing that is not terminated stays effective on the record and will be found by the next funder's search, so the practical cost of the $165.78 is a stalled transaction, not $165.78.

questions.prompt: A merchant is notified that a 45 percent participation exists and is told to split its monthly payment. It asks you whether it can keep paying the servicer. What is the honest answer, and what document resolves it?
questions.answer: It can keep paying the party it has been paying until a notification that reasonably identifies the assigned rights arrives, and after that it must pay the assignee; where the notification asks for less than the full instalment, the merchant may refuse the split and pay the full amount to one assignee, so the document that resolves the question is a single notification for the full instalment with proof of assignment attached.
questions.distractor: It can keep paying the servicer because a participation is an internal arrangement between funders that does not change the merchant's payment obligation.
questions.correction: A participation is internal until it is notified, and after notification it is not. The risk this creates is not theoretical: a merchant that pays the old collection point after a valid notification pays twice, and the amount at stake is the participant's share of every month in the gap, $105,300.00 over three months on a $78,000.00 monthly flow. The advisor's job is to get the notice, the proof and the payment direction into one document before the first split month.

questions.prompt: A renewal rolls a $57,960.00 balance and $60,000.00 of new money into a $117,960.00 base at 1.36 with a 3 percent fee taken from the new money. The broker calls it a 1.36 deal. Write the two sentences that correct him.
questions.answer: The merchant receives $58,200.00 and owes $102,465.60 more than the balance, which is 176.06 per $100 of new money; the 1.36 applies to money already spent as well as money received, and the only honest comparison is the incremental obligation against the cash that moves.
questions.distractor: The 1.36 factor applies to the whole base, so the deal is priced at $36.00 per $100 and the merchant should compare it with the 1.38 on the original advance and conclude that the renewal is cheaper.
questions.correction: Comparing 1.36 with 1.38 compares two prices on different quantities of money. The original 1.38 bought $120,000.00 of cash; the renewal's 1.36 buys $58,200.00 of cash and re-prices $57,960.00 that was already spent, adding $20,865.60 to that balance before the new money is counted. A merchant who is told the factor has fallen has been told something true and misleading.

questions.prompt: A merchant with 92.65 percent debits to deposits and a 1.69 day turnover wants a Monday debit. What do you measure, and what do you recommend?
questions.answer: Measure the day's debits against the settlements available that morning, including the T+2 lag on card receipts, and recommend a day after the largest settlement batch lands, because a 1.69 day turnover means the balance is a timing artefact and $42,820.00 of weekend settlements will not be there on Monday.
questions.distractor: Measure the monthly coverage ratio, which is 70.89 percent of net cash, and recommend the Monday debit because the monthly figure shows the merchant can afford it.
questions.correction: The monthly ratio measures capacity and the daily calendar measures the return. A 70.89 percent coverage ratio on a 1.69 day turnover is a file that will run clean for months and then return an entry on a holiday week, and the return is what triggers fees, the default clause and the collections process. Choosing the debit day is a cash-management decision that belongs in the recommendation.

questions.prompt: A contract accelerates at will, waives a jury, and requires arbitration 1,900 miles away with a $12,500.00 deposit against a $9,400.00 claim. What may you say, and what may you not say?
questions.answer: You may describe what each clause does, quantify the dispute cost at $31,950.00 and the 3.40 to 1 ratio, and recommend that the merchant have counsel read the forum clause before signing; you may not opine that the clauses are void or that the merchant will win, because acceleration at will is construed rather than struck and arbitration is generally enforced.
questions.distractor: You may tell the merchant the clauses are unenforceable, because a clause that makes a $9,400.00 claim cost $31,950.00 to bring is unconscionable as a matter of law.
questions.correction: Unconscionability is a defence argued on facts, and the answer depends on the merchant, the bargaining history and the jurisdiction. What an advisor can do without a law licence is arithmetic and disclosure: state the deposit, the distance, the counsel estimate, the travel, the total and the ratio, and say plainly that whether the clause holds is a question for a lawyer where the contract is governed.

questions.prompt: Three statement PDFs share a creation timestamp, the operating account is 41 days old, revenue rose 240.05 percent and the return shows exactly $116,400.00 more than the statements. The merchant offers to explain. What happens next?
questions.answer: The submission stops, the indicators are recorded with their measurements and dates, the explanation is noted rather than solicited, and the file goes no further; the advisor does not ask for the missing statements, does not describe the merchant as a fraudster in writing, and does not mention any report a bank may or may not file.
questions.distractor: The advisor takes the explanation, asks for the statements that close the $116,400.00 gap, and submits once the deposits reconcile to the return, because a reconciled file is what underwriting needs.
questions.correction: The request for reconciling documents is the misconduct, not the submission. It tells the merchant which measurement failed, and the next version of the file will pass that measurement. The other two prohibitions are equally practical: a written accusation creates defamation exposure, and any statement about a report filed by a financial institution is prohibited by the tipping-off rule.

questions.prompt: A complaint alleges a debit eleven days after payoff, another alleges an undisclosed fee, and a third alleges a call after an opt-out. Write the response plan and the process changes, and say what the 1.40 per 100 files rate does and does not tell you.
questions.answer: Acknowledge each within three business days, preserve the authorisation, the payoff quote, the wire confirmation, the disclosure version and the opt-out record, answer the facts without admissions, and change three processes: cancel the authorisation at payoff, version-control the disclosure, and test the opt-out mechanism after day thirty; the rate tells you the volume and nothing about the causes, which are three different failures.
questions.distractor: Acknowledge each complaint, explain the contract terms, and record the 1.40 per 100 files rate as within tolerance, since three complaints across 214 files is a low base rate and each has a contractual explanation.
questions.correction: A low rate with three distinct causes is a control failure that has not yet produced volume. The debit after payoff is the serious one because it is a payment taken when no obligation existed, and the remedy is a cancellation step in the payoff procedure, not a better explanation. The fee complaint points at a disclosure that was not the version in force, and the call complaint points at a test that was never run.

questions.prompt: At day ninety the bank shows fifteen debits, two returns and $140.00 of bank fees, and the servicer's ledger shows $66,924.00 collected against thirteen expected debits of $5,148.00. What reconciles, what does not, and what is the exception?
questions.answer: The net bank movement of $66,924.00 reconciles to thirteen debits, but the two $50.00 return fees were collected and never credited, so the ledger overstates the balance by $100.00; the $140.00 of bank fees is the merchant's own cost and is not part of the obligation.
questions.distractor: Everything reconciles because $77,220.00 less $10,296.00 equals $66,924.00, and the fees are within the tolerance the audit sets for items under $250.00.
questions.correction: Gross debits less returns is the bank's number, not the contract's. The contract adds the return fee to the balance, so a ledger that ignores the collection leaves a small unexplained residual that will surface at payoff as a shortfall, and a shortfall is what stops a termination statement twenty days later. Tolerances belong in the audit plan, but a fee that changes the balance is never immaterial.

questions.prompt: You are handed a file where the settlement sheet omits the escrow from the deducted column and the comparison sheet divides total repayment by the approved amount. Which measure is wrong and by how much, and what is the second error?
questions.answer: The comparison sheet's denominator is wrong: $51,000.00 over $150,000.00 gives $34.00 per $100, while over $96,292.95 it gives $52.96, so the sheet understates the price by $18.96 per $100; the second error is treating the $7,500.00 escrow as neither deducted nor available, which understates the merchant's liquidity by the same amount.
questions.distractor: The denominators agree because the factor is applied to the approved amount, so $34.00 per $100 is the contractual price and the escrow is a timing item that does not affect any measure.
questions.correction: The factor is applied to the approved amount, and that is precisely why the approved amount is the wrong denominator for the merchant's cost. Cost per $100 of net is the only measure that answers the question the merchant is asking. The escrow omission is a separate failure: it disappears from both columns, which means the sheet neither prices it nor returns it.

questions.prompt: A file funded on 7 November is audited on 6 February after thirteen weekly debits. Name the three records the audit must reconcile and the one event that would make the whole schedule unenforceable.
questions.answer: The bank statement, the servicer's ledger and the contract's amortisation must reconcile, with fee lines shown separately from principal; the event that would undermine the schedule is an authorisation that does not name the party debiting the account after an assignment, because an unauthorised entry is returnable and the returns then feed the default clause.
questions.distractor: The bank statement and the ledger are enough, since the contract's schedule is fixed at closing and the only question is whether the merchant paid; an authorisation issue is a bank matter rather than a funding matter.
questions.correction: The contract is the third ledger, and it is the one that decides whether the fees collected were owed. The authorisation point is the audit's most valuable finding because it is cheap to fix at day ninety and expensive to discover at day three hundred, when a block of entries is returned as unauthorised and the funder's remedy is the default clause rather than a corrected form.
